e.etymology: A Spanish-language spelling of Asenath, the Egyptian wife of Joseph in Genesis. The name is thought to be Egyptian for belonging to the goddess Neith.
A spelling of Laken, a modern American name built on the word lake, first noticed through a character on the 1980s soap opera Santa Barbara. Layken is the heroine of Colleen Hoover's novel Slammed.
A modern American coinage with the popular Ja- beginning, close in sound to Jabari, Jamari and Zachary. It has no established meaning.
A recent name popular in India and in Indian American families. Its source is unclear; it is often linked with Amira, Arabic for princess.
A modern American name, probably shortened from Cambria, the Latin name for Wales, and shaped like Aubrie and Brie.
In Indian use, the title of the saint Sai Baba of Shirdi, a word for a holy man that is often placed before another name, as in Sai Krishna. Sai is also a Japanese given name.

assoc.t: sai, the three-pronged dagger of martial arts

e.meaning: mountain ibexes, an image of grace
e.etymology: From Arabic arwa, female mountain goats or ibexes, an image of grace and agility. Arwa al-Sulayhi ruled Yemen as queen in the 11th and 12th centuries.
An Indian name from Sanskrit ahan, day, taken to mean dawn or the first light of morning.
A modern American coinage that joins Ren, or the bird name Wren, to the popular -lee ending, as in Wrenley and Brinlee.
An English surname from places called Kenton, from the Old English personal name Cena, or cyne, royal, with tun, settlement.
A spelling of Melody, the English word for a tune, from Greek meloidia, singing. Mélodie is the French form.
The medieval Scandinavian form of Helen, on record in Sweden and Norway since the 1300s. Helen is Greek, probably from a word for torch. Elin is also a Welsh form of the same name.
namesakes: Elin Hilderbrand (bestselling novelist of Nantucket summer stories)
Elin Nordegren (Swedish former model, ex-wife of Tiger Woods)

e.etymology: The Scottish spelling of Isabel, a medieval Spanish and Occitan form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath.
A modern spelling in the family of Aliya and Aaliyah, from Arabic ali, high or exalted. Some families say it like Alaya.
A modern American name, a form of Zaria with the -iya ending of Aaliyah. Zaria matches the Slavic word zarya, dawn, and the name of a city in northern Nigeria.
A modern name with a Hawaiian sound, close to Kalea and Leia. Its own meaning is not established.
A medieval diminutive of Jane, the feminine form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. It was chiefly Scottish until the 1800s and peaked in the United States in the 1940s.
namesakes: Janet Yellen (Federal Reserve chair and Treasury secretary)

assoc.t: Janet Jackson, pop and R&B superstar
Janet, the all-knowing helper on The Good Place

e.etymology: An elaboration of Jane with the ending of Alice and Bernice, introduced by American author Paul Leicester Ford in his 1899 novel Janice Meredith. Jane goes back to Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
namesakes: Janice Soprano (Tony's sister on The Sopranos)

assoc.t: Janice, Chandler's on-and-off girlfriend on Friends

e.etymology: A spelling of Caden, a modern American name that rose in the 1990s and 2000s alongside Aiden, Jaden and Braden. Caden is also an Irish surname, from Mac Cadain.
A spelling of Nia, Swahili for purpose and the name of the fifth principle of Kwanzaa. The Swahili word comes from Arabic niyya, intention. Nia is also a Welsh name, a form of Irish Niamh.
A respelling of Micah, the Biblical prophet, whose name is a short form of Hebrew Mikhayahu, who is like Yahweh?
A Biblical Hebrew name, Yachaziel, meaning God sees. Several men bear it in Chronicles, among them a Levite who prophesies victory to King Jehoshaphat.
From Old Norse Runi, tied to run, a secret or a runic letter, and runi, a confidant. It is a common man's name in Scandinavia, and in English it matches the word rune.

assoc.t: rune, a letter of the ancient Germanic alphabets

e.etymology: A compound of Emma and Lee that sounds the same as Emily. Emma comes from Germanic ermen, whole or universal; Lee is from an Old English word for a meadow or clearing.
A modern American name that sets Grace in the shape of Grayson and Mason. Grace is the English word, from Latin gratia, first taken up as a name by the Puritans.
A Yiddish pet form of Shaina or Shaindel, from sheyn, beautiful. It is used mainly in Orthodox and Hasidic Jewish families.
From Hebrew Adonai, my Lord, the word spoken in place of the name of God in Jewish prayer and scripture reading.

assoc.t: Adonai, a Hebrew name for God

e.note: Adonai is a name of God in Jewish prayer; many Jews would find it unsuitable as a child's name.

e.etymology: An English surname used as a first name. Its recent use follows Taysom Hill, the New Orleans Saints player who starred at Brigham Young University.
namesakes: Taysom Hill (New Orleans Saints quarterback and all-purpose player)

assoc.t: NFL player Taysom Hill of the New Orleans Saints

e.etymology: A spelling of Tommy, the pet form of Thomas, from Aramaic te'oma, twin. This spelling has long been given to girls as well as boys.
namesakes: Tommie Smith (sprinter who raised his fist on the 1968 Olympic podium)

e.etymology: A spelling of Damian, from the Greek name Damianos, derived from damao, to tame. Saints Cosmas and Damian were early Christian brothers honored as physicians.

assoc.t: sounds like Damien, the devil child in The Omen

e.etymology: Made famous by singer Shania Twain, born Eilleen Edwards, who took it as her stage name in the early 1990s. It is often said to be Ojibwe for I'm on my way, but that claim is disputed.
namesakes: Shania Twain (country-pop singer of Man! I Feel Like a Woman!)

e.etymology: The Hebrew form of Aaron, brother of Moses and first high priest of Israel. Its meaning is not known; suggestions include exalted and high mountain, and an Egyptian source is possible.
